templates.pattern: A network receives [DATA] MB of data in [TIME] seconds. Calculate the throughput of the network in MB/s.
templates.explanation:
Throughput = data received ÷ time
= [DATA] ÷ [TIME]
= [RESULT] MB/s

Throughput is the actual data transfer rate achieved — it is always less than or equal to bandwidth due to overhead, errors and congestion.

templates.pattern: A packet has a total size of [TOTAL] bytes of which [OH] bytes are header overhead. Calculate the protocol overhead as a percentage of the total packet size.
templates.explanation:
Protocol overhead % = (header size ÷ total packet size) × 100
= ([OH] ÷ [TOTAL]) × 100
= [RESULT]%

Smaller packets have proportionally more overhead. A 20-byte header on a 40-byte packet is 50% overhead but only 1.3% on a 1500-byte packet.

templates.pattern: A [TOTAL] MB/s link carries [OH] MB/s of protocol overhead. Calculate the effective data rate in MB/s.
templates.explanation:
Effective data rate = total bandwidth − overhead
= [TOTAL] − [OH]
= [RESULT] MB/s

Not all bandwidth carries useful data. Protocol headers, acknowledgements and retransmissions all reduce the effective data rate available to applications.

templates.pattern: A signal travels from a sender to a receiver with a propagation delay of [PROP] ms. Calculate the round trip time (RTT) in ms.
templates.explanation:
Round Trip Time = 2 × propagation delay
= 2 × [PROP]
= [RESULT] ms

RTT measures the time for a signal to travel to the destination and back. It is used in TCP to set timeout values and measure network performance.

templates.pattern: A network receives [N] data values: [V1], [V2], [V3] and [V4]. Calculate the checksum by summing all values.
templates.explanation:
Checksum = sum of all data values
= [V1] + [V2] + [V3] + [V4]
= [RESULT]

The sender calculates the checksum and sends it with the data. The receiver recalculates and compares — if different an error has occurred. Simple checksums cannot detect all types of errors.

templates.pattern: A subnet has [N] host bits in its subnet mask. Calculate the maximum number of usable host addresses on this subnet.
templates.explanation:
Usable hosts = 2ⁿ − 2
= 2^[N] − 2
= [2^N] − 2
= [RESULT]

Two addresses are reserved — the network address (all host bits 0) and the broadcast address (all host bits 1). A /24 subnet with 8 host bits gives 2⁸ − 2 = 254 usable hosts.

templates.pattern: A network uses [N] bits for subnetting. Calculate the number of subnets that can be created.
templates.explanation:
Number of subnets = 2ⁿ
= 2^[N]
= [RESULT]

Each additional subnet bit doubles the number of available subnets but halves the number of hosts per subnet. Network designers must balance subnet count against hosts per subnet.

templates.pattern: A network uses CIDR notation with a prefix length of /[PREFIX]. Calculate the total number of IP addresses in this network.
templates.explanation:
Total IP addresses = 2^(32 − prefix)
= 2^(32 − [PREFIX])
= 2^[32-PREFIX]
= [RESULT]

A /24 network has 2⁸ = 256 addresses. A /16 has 2¹⁶ = 65,536. The prefix tells us how many bits are the network portion — the rest are for hosts.

templates.pattern: A network switch has [PORTS] ports. Each port connects to a single device. Calculate the total number of devices in the collision domain if all ports are in the same VLAN.
templates.explanation:
Devices in collision domain = number of ports
= [PORTS]
= [RESULT]

A switch creates a separate collision domain per port — unlike a hub where all devices share one collision domain. However all devices on the same VLAN share a broadcast domain.

templates.pattern: A router receives a packet with destination IP address [IP] and subnet mask with [BITS] host bits. Calculate the network address by finding IP − (IP mod 2^[BITS]).
templates.explanation:
Network address = IP − (IP mod 2^host_bits)
= [IP] − ([IP] mod 2^[BITS])
= [IP] − [HOST]
= [RESULT]

The network address has all host bits set to zero. It identifies the network and cannot be assigned to a device.
